title: Cache Invalidation
description: Tackle the 'two hard problems' of computer science — TTL strategies, write-through vs write-behind, cache stampede, and probabilistic early expiration.

segments.text: There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. That joke exists because keeping a cache in sync with the source of truth is genuinely one of the hardest problems in systems engineering.

The core problem is simple. You cache a value. The underlying data changes. Now your cache serves stale data. Users see outdated prices, old profile pictures, or incorrect inventory counts. Staleness erodes trust.

The simplest invalidation strategy is TTL — time to live. Set a cache entry to expire after sixty seconds. After that, the next request fetches fresh data. Short TTLs mean fresher data but more database load. Long TTLs mean staler data but less load.

Write-through caching updates the cache and the database simultaneously on every write. The cache is always up to date. The tradeoff? Every write is slower because it hits two stores. But reads are consistently fast and fresh.

Write-behind — also called write-back — writes to the cache immediately and asynchronously updates the database later. Writes are incredibly fast, but if the cache crashes before flushing to the database, you lose data.
Write-through for consistency. Write-behind for speed. TTL-based expiry for simplicity. In practice, most systems use a combination — TTL as a safety net with explicit invalidation on writes.
segments.thought_prompt: For an e-commerce product catalog, would you use write-through or write-behind? What about for a shopping cart?

segments.text: Cache stampede — also called thundering herd — happens when a popular cache entry expires. Hundreds of requests simultaneously miss the cache and all hit the database at once. The database buckles under the sudden load.

You can prevent stampedes with locking. Only one request fetches from the database and rebuilds the cache. Others wait for the fresh value. Another approach: background refresh — proactively rebuild the cache before it expires.

Probabilistic early expiration is clever. Each request checks: should I refresh this entry early? The probability increases as the TTL approaches zero. This staggers refreshes over time so they don't all happen at once.

When data changes, should you delete the cache entry or update it? Deletion is safer — the next read will fetch fresh data. Updating risks race conditions where two concurrent writers leave the cache in an inconsistent state.
The pattern 'delete on write, populate on read' — called cache-aside — is the most common and safest approach. It's simple, avoids race conditions, and naturally handles cache failures gracefully.
segments.thought_prompt: In cache-aside, what happens if the delete succeeds but the database write fails? How would you handle this?

segments.text: Cache invalidation is hard because distributed state is hard. Use TTLs as safety nets, choose your write strategy based on consistency requirements, protect against stampedes, and prefer deletion over updating. Master these patterns and caching becomes your superpower.
